# Phase 1 report: a 1930s semi in London

*Generated by `npm run report` from `data/register.json` and the PVGIS snapshot. Do not edit by hand.*

This report compares a gas combi boiler with an air source heat pump for one house, with honest ranges. The numbers are estimates for a typical house of this kind, not advice for any particular home, and not financial advice.

## The house

A semi-detached house built 1930–49, in London: 90 m² over two storeys, unfilled cavity walls, 100 mm of loft insulation and retrofitted double glazing. This is the main case; the variant with no loft insulation is not reported here.

- Heat loss coefficient (central): 302 W/K.
- Mean internal air temperature (central): 15.7 °C, held continuously.
- Prices: the Ofgem price cap, GB average by Direct Debit, for 1 October–31 December 2026. Electricity 26.32p a kWh and 54.83p a day; gas 7.97p a kWh and 29.68p a day. The heat pump house has no gas supply, so it pays no gas standing charge.
- Carbon: 0.18296 kgCO₂e a kWh of gas and 0.14396 kgCO₂e a kWh of grid electricity (annual average).

## Gas boiler versus heat pump

Both setups run on the same samples, so each sample compares the same house and household with different kit. The difference is gas minus heat pump: a positive cost difference means the heat pump is cheaper to run, and a positive carbon difference means it emits less.

| Gas minus heat pump, a year | Central | Median | 10th to 90th percentile |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Running cost | £50 | £60 | −£170 to £220 |
| Carbon (kgCO₂e) | 1,800 kg | 1,720 kg | 1,420 kg to 2,020 kg |

**The heat pump is cheaper to run in 65% of samples** (rounded to the nearest 5%; an exact tie counts as half). With 500 samples, this share is uncertain by about ±4 percentage points (95% confidence).

**This running-cost comparison leans in the heat pump’s favour.** One calibrated mean internal temperature, taken from gas-heated homes, applies to both setups. Heat pump households often heat for longer, so the heat pump’s running cost is likely too low here, and the share of samples in which it is cheaper too high ([issue 15](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/15)). Phase 2 is where this gets addressed.

## Sensitivity

Each uncertain row is run at its low and then its high value, with every other row at its default. The rows are ranked by how much they move the cost difference.

At the central values, a kWh of heat costs almost the same from either system: 9.38p from the boiler (7.97p ÷ 0.85) and 9.40p from the heat pump (26.32p ÷ 2.8). So rows that change how much heat the house needs, such as fabric quality or the temperature, move both running costs by hundreds of pounds but barely move the difference. The difference turns on the SPF and the boiler efficiency, and on the gas standing charge the heat pump house does not pay. Base electricity use moves both setups equally.

The low and high are the ends of each row’s range, not percentiles. For the heat pump SPF, they are the clip limits of its lognormal distribution, far out in its tails, so its row shows an extreme spread.

| Row | Low to high | Gas boiler cost | Heat pump cost | Gas minus heat pump |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Air source heat pump seasonal performance factor (space heat and hot water combined) | 2 to 4 | £2,010 | £2,400 to £1,630 | −£390 to £380 |
| Gas combi boiler seasonal efficiency (space heat and hot water) | 0.8 to 0.89 | £2,080 to £1,970 | £1,960 | £120 to £10 |
| Fabric quality factor (one multiplier on every U-value and the air change rate) | 0.75 to 1.15 | £1,720 to £2,190 | £1,660 to £2,140 | £50 |
| Mean internal air temperature, heated continuously (calibrated to measured gas use) | 14.5 to 16.8 °C | £1,840 to £2,190 | £1,780 to £2,140 | £50 |
| Hot water use | 70 to 140 litres/day | £1,960 to £2,080 | £1,910 to £2,020 | £50 |
| Internal gains (occupants, lighting, appliances, cooking), constant | 350 to 550 W | £2,060 to £1,960 | £2,010 to £1,910 | £50 |
| Base electricity use (lights and appliances), the same in both setups | 1,600 to 3,800 kWh/year | £1,780 to £2,350 | £1,720 to £2,300 | £50 |

## How the ranges are made

- **Samples:** 500 joint samples with seed 1. Each sample draws a value for every uncertain row: fabric quality factor; internal gains; mean internal air temperature, heated continuously; gas combi boiler seasonal efficiency; air source heat pump seasonal performance factor; hot water use; base electricity use. Every other number is fixed.
- **Stable draws:** each value comes from a hash of the seed, the sample number and the row id, passed through the row’s inverse distribution function. Triangular rows use their default as the mode. The SPF is lognormal and clipped to its low and high.
- **Central** is the run with every row at its default. **Median** and the **10th to 90th percentile** come from the samples (linear interpolation between ranked samples).
- **Fabric quality** is one shared factor on every U-value and the air change rate. The other rows are drawn independently of each other.
- **Rounding:** costs to £10, energy to 100 kWh, carbon to 10 kg and shares to 5%.

## Benchmark and calibration

The benchmark checked annual **space heat** against the government’s Home Energy Model (HEM), using a rough calculation for the same house, before the engine was built. The rule set in advance: proceed if within 15%, add thermal mass between 15% and 30%, and stop above 30%.

- **The pre-registered check missed the rule.** HEM gave 15,500 kWh at its own settings (about 18.8 °C of air), and the rough calculation at 18 °C of air gave 13,000 kWh: a gap of −15.7%, just outside 15%.
- **The rule was amended after seeing that result** (Magnus, 17 October 2026). HEM’s thermostat controls the felt (operative) temperature, which runs below the air temperature, while this engine uses air temperature. So the check compares like with like: at about 17.8 °C of air, HEM gives 13,700 kWh, a gap of −4.6%. **Decision: proceed with no thermal mass.** A test keeps the engine itself within 10% of that HEM run.
- **Both models predict more gas than comparable homes use.** NEED gives 10,980 to 15,433 kWh of gas a year. **Decision: calibrate the mean internal temperature** so the central gas use hits the midpoint, 13,200 kWh, a target fixed before the engine existed. Here the central gas use is 13,100 kWh.
- The full write-up is in [scripts/benchmark/README.md](../scripts/benchmark/README.md), and the decisions are in the [calibration ADR](../REFERENCE/decisions/2026-10-17-air-temperature-calibrated-to-need.md).

## Limitations

- **One calibrated temperature applies to both setups.** It comes from gas-heated homes, and heat pump households often heat for longer, so the heat pump’s running cost is biased low ([issue 15](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/15)). It may also absorb errors in the default U-values ([issue 14](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/14)).
- **No thermal mass, and continuous heating** to one temperature ([issue 13](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/13)).
- **One SPF for the whole year.** The heat pump has no capacity limit and no backup heater; its performance in cold weather is phase 2 work.
- **Fixed prices and one typical weather year** ([issue 16](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/16)), and an **annual average grid carbon factor** ([issue 17](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/17)).
- **The boiler’s own pump and fan electricity is left out** ([issue 18](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/18)).
- **Uncertain rows other than fabric quality are drawn independently**, so a real link between them (for example, more occupants means more hot water and more internal gains) is not captured ([issue 20](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues/20)).
- **Constant internal gains**, and windows split equally over four orientations.
- Several register rows still need a line-by-line check against their source ([issues 7, 8 and 9](https://github.com/mannepanne/energy-sim/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3Atechnical-debt)).
